VI. The principle that the nobler possible being comes before the lower one
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00700

Here is another principle: a possible being that is nobler must come earlier in the order of existence than a less noble possible being. If the less noble one exists, the nobler one must already have existed. This is a powerful principle with many uses. We have made much use of it, by God’s grace. Aristotle’s school used it often in Theology of Aristotle and On the Heavens and the World. Avicenna built his account of the order of existence and of the outward and return paths on it. The Illuminationist philosopher Suhrawardī developed it in many books. He used it to prove the existence of intellects and of immaterial forms—the guardians of natural kinds. Muhammad al-Shahrazūrī later explained the principle in detail.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00701

Here is the proof, following Suhrawardī. If a lower possible being comes from God, a nobler possible being must have come before it. If it came at the same level, two things would come directly from the One at once, one nobler and one lower. If it came after the lower being through that being, the effect would be nobler than its cause. If it could not come before, at the same time, or after, then a possible being would never exist. But if it is possible, there must be a cause for its existence outside its own nature. The cause cannot be lower than God or any of the effects that come from Him. Otherwise it would have to be nobler than the cause that produced the lower being. So the possible nobler being must come from God before the lower one, and the chain of causes must proceed from the noblest to the lower, step by step.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00702

Suhrawardī’s commentator arranges the choices this way: Suppose a lower possible being exists but a nobler one has not preceded it. Four unacceptable consequences may follow. If the lower being exists through the nobler one, the original supposition is false. If both can come directly from God, many things come from the One in the same respect. If the nobler one comes through a lower effect, its cause would be less noble than its effect. If it can come neither from God nor from His effects, something nobler than God would be required. Every choice is impossible. So the nobler being must already exist before the lower one. Nothing is nobler than God or His act; therefore, the noblest possible effects are closest to Him, and the causes between Him and lower beings must follow this same order.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00703

A key note on this principle: some writers say it applies only to beings of the same kind, and only to beings above the changing physical world. But existence is one simple reality, with differences of greater and lesser perfection. These differences can give rise to different kinds of things, or to different individuals within one kind. The second kind of difference occurs only among changing things that can develop new abilities. Since all possible beings share the one reality of existence, the rule can prove that every higher level of existence must come before a lower one, even when they do not belong to the same kind.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00704

The second limit does matter. Otherwise we might wrongly conclude that every person must receive every kind of perfection, even though many people do not reach their full intellectual or bodily abilities. This rule applies to possible beings whose existence lasts as long as their causes last, beyond the effects of heavenly motions and physical conditions. It applies where nothing blocks the cause. In the changing world, other causes can prevent a being from reaching a higher state. A physical thing may be capable of many perfections in itself but be kept from them by other things, depending on its readiness and on the motions of the heavens. But for lasting, immaterial beings, their higher or lower rank follows the rank of their cause. This explains where the principle applies and where it does not.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00705

A lower thing in the changing world can come before a higher thing in time and in its natural development. A seed comes before a tree, an egg before a chicken, and an embryo before a mature animal. But when we look at what causes them to exist, the higher thing comes first. What is actual comes before what is only possible. The more perfect being is prior in the order of making; the less perfect one comes later. The same is true in other pairs: necessity before possibility, the particular before the general, the defining feature before the broad kind, the individual before the kind, form before matter, unity before multiplicity, continuity before separation, existence before non-existence, good before evil, and truth before falsehood.

A difficult objection is raised. The proof seems to mix what is possible or impossible in itself with what is possible or impossible in relation to something else. Perhaps a being that is impossible in itself could still be possible in relation to a nobler possible being, without being made possible by that being. The higher level that lies beyond God’s own perfection may be impossible in itself, the critic says, yet possible in relation to a nobler possible being that calls for it.

passage-en-00707

Dawānī states the objection this way in his commentary on The Temples: the proof fails unless the possibility of an effect requires the possibility of its cause. But it seems possible for the first effect not to exist, even though the nonexistence of its cause, God, is impossible. Dawānī answers that considering the effect by itself shows that nothing in it makes it impossible. But this answer does not settle the question.

passage-en-00708

He then gives another version: if a possible nobler being did not exist before a lower possible being, it would not be possible. For if it did exist, it would either come directly from God, though the lower one already does; or it would come through the lower one, which would make the cause lower than its effect. Both are impossible. So the higher being’s possibility would make it impossible—a contradiction. The same difficulty remains: the answer works only if “impossible” includes “impossible because of another thing.” If it means “impossible in itself,” it does not work.

I answer that possibility follows from existence. What is made real by a cause is the existence of a thing; then the mind considers that existent thing and forms the idea of its nature. We call that nature “possible” when we think of it apart from existence and non-existence. So kinds of things and their possibilities follow the order of what actually exists. Every chain of existence ends in God. There can be no possible thing whose existence, if it were real, would depend on something impossible in itself. That would be a baseless guess.

passage-en-00710

There is another way to answer. God, who exists necessarily through Himself, cannot lack any degree of perfection or nobility. Every real perfection and every active, positive feature of existence must be in Him in a higher and nobler way. If we imagine a rank of goodness or perfection above what belongs to God, careful thought shows that it must already be in Him. There can be no possible or impossible feature in God alongside His necessary existence, because that would make Him complex. Every perfection that a possible being can call for must therefore be in God or in something that depends on Him. God is necessary in every respect of existence that can be found in anything. His one reality is complete and beyond complete in every perfection, with unlimited strength and creative power—far beyond what any intellect can grasp.

passage-en-00711

No holy intellect can fully survey these ranks of perfection, long for all of them in detail, or contain them in its own understanding. Reason can prove that they belong to God, but it cannot picture their full extent.

passage-en-00712

We cannot imagine any degree of greatness, honor, or endlessness—whether in strength, number, or duration—that is absent from God's simple reality. If a perfection is found anywhere, it must exist in Him in a higher and nobler way, through the necessity of His own being. As argued earlier, every positive aspect of existence belongs to Him not by addition or chance, but necessarily through what He is.

This shows that the proof does not confuse what is possible in itself with what is possible in relation to something else. Dawānī’s own answer to the familiar objection—that a possible effect could fail to exist, even though that would mean its cause did not exist—also fails. Possibility in relation to another applies only when there is no necessary link between the two things. A cause must exist in relation to its effect, and the effect must follow from its cause. Each is necessary in relation to the other.

passage-en-00714

The true answer, as I have explained, is that an effect is a way of existing that follows necessarily from its cause. Possibility belongs to a thing’s nature when we consider it by itself, and that nature is not linked to its cause as either existing or not existing. Its possibility therefore entails neither that its cause exists nor that it does not. But when we consider the existence of the thing, that existence is necessarily dependent on God. To imagine that it does not exist would be to affirm both existence and non-existence of the same thing. So a possible nature does not entail an impossible result; the supposed impossible result is impossible in itself.

A puzzle once troubled me about this principle. The intellects are pure lights, all sharing the simple reality of light but differing in strength and weakness, as the Persian and Illuminationist philosophers say. In my own account, they are pure forms of existence, sharing one reality and differing in strength. Either way, there would have to be infinitely many levels between any two intellects, and between God, the Light of Lights, and the first intellect. Since they share one reality, there should always be another rank of light between any two ranks: stronger than the lower one and weaker than the higher one. The rule of the nobler possible being would require every such rank to exist. That would place endlessly many intellects between each pair of intellects, all ordered in levels. This seems impossible. It would also make one endless chain lie between two fixed points.

passage-en-00716

I put this puzzle to many learned people of our time, but no one could solve it. Then God lit my heart and opened my sight to the kingdom of heaven and earth through knowledge of myself. Knowledge of the self is the key to the hidden world. When I looked within, I found a simple, self-aware existence. It was not a body, an organ, or a bodily spirit, and it did not contain a mental idea or an abstract nature. All these things can disappear from my awareness; my own self cannot disappear from itself. I also saw that my self was not limited to one fixed rank. Though one and simple, it can understand ideas, imagine images, and sense things through itself.

passage-en-00717

The mind does not understand or imagine only through tools that act in its place. If the eye or ear were the true knower, then the person using the eye or ear would not know what it was doing. The eye and ear would be separate animals joined to our body. The senses help cause particular experiences, but the self is what knows through them. We will explain this more fully in the discussion of the soul.

The human self, though one in its existence, has levels: intellect, imagination, and sense. Each level has degrees of greater or lesser strength. One person’s sight may be stronger than another’s; one person’s imagination clearer; one person’s intellect more complete. So a simple being can contain many levels without being many beings.

passage-en-00719

The intellects are even more clearly like this. Each intellect has, within its one existence, many possible ranks and limits. The highest rank is just below the lowest rank of the intellect above it; the lowest rank is just above the highest rank of the intellect below it. These are not separate beings arranged between two others, but levels held together in one complete existence. If you ask what these intellects are in relation to God, they are all ranks of the divine order and lights of His presence. Their many effects—heavenly spheres and other simple or complex beings—do not divide them. Their degrees of strength, nearness, and perfection explain why each produces higher or lower kinds of nature and bodies. Their lasting existence through God does not prevent the changing world from beginning in time.

The intellects have no beginning in their own order of existence. But in relation to the new things they produce, they change along with those things. A cause exists with its effect in the respect in which it causes that effect. As new effects come to be, this relation is renewed. The way something that does not change in itself can be related to changing things is difficult for many people to grasp, but clear to those whom God has helped.

Here is another point. Existence has two extremes: God, whose perfection and power are without limit, and first matter, which has the least perfection and the greatest readiness to receive form. Existence cannot reach first matter without passing through all the levels between them. Nor can it rise from matter toward God without passing through every middle level in order. Once this is clear, we can prove many middle levels not only through the rule of the nobler possible being but also through a second rule, which we may call the rule of the lower possible being.

By the first rule we can prove that earth and the other simple elements have an intellectual guide and a form in the world of images. By the rule of the lower possible being, we can then show that they also have plant-like souls, life, and imagination in the world between intellect and matter. The same rule shows that a body capable of direct movement comes after the animal soul and before circular movement, which is an added quality.

passage-en-00723

Plants also have a basic nature that preserves their structure and balance. This nature works on matter through the plant soul. These powers are not qualities added to a body, as people usually think, but beings whose existence is joined to what they can do.

VII. What follows from the principles established so far
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter

God’s being is perfect, fully active, and necessary, with no trace of absence or lack. So the first thing to come from Him must be the noblest being that has no trace of absence or lack. It must belong to the world of intellect, not the world of souls, still less the world of nature.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00726

A soul contains two kinds of absence. One is an absence that exists only when the mind analyzes it. It has no separate reality outside the mind. The mind considers any created being, except the fully simple reality of God, and separates its existence from the particular limit that gives it this form. A soul can then seem made up of existence and non-existence, completeness and lack, good and evil, light and darkness, necessity and possibility, nature and individual existence. But in reality its absence is swallowed up by its existence, its evil by its good, its lack by its completeness, its darkness by its light, and its possibility by necessity. Its nature is held within its actual existence. These are only ways the mind considers it; there is no real absence, evil, lack, darkness, possibility, or separate nature in God.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00727

The second kind is real absence: the lack within a thing that is still developing. A soul is actual in one way, but still has a perfection it may gain. If it had no perfection left to reach, it would already be an intellect, not a soul. So a soul is partly actual and partly only possible. It cannot be the first thing after God.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00728

Natural forms that depend on matter are even further from being the first effect. They contain the two kinds of absence found in souls, and a third: their existence depends on matter in two different ways. Matter is the readiness through which a form comes to be, and the form is one of the causes that makes matter actual. The first kind of absence is the potential existence of what has not yet come to be; the second is the matter that comes before the form. The first is prior in nature; the second is prior in its own being. A natural form is surrounded by these two kinds of absence at every moment because it comes into being and continues through stages.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00729

A soul differs from a natural form because it remains the same in its own nature while its link to a body changes. It has both an intellectual, lasting aspect and a changing aspect through which it governs the body. A natural form, by contrast, is itself a changing link to matter.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00730

A body’s measurable shape has even more kinds of absence. It lacks the fullest perfection, it lacks the perfection it may later gain, it is absent from itself at different times, and it is absent from itself in different places. Matter considered before it receives any particular form is the capacity to receive one.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00731

Aristotle counts the absence of a form among the three principles involved when things come into being, alongside form and matter. The absence before a new thing comes to be is joined to the earlier part of its matter. Matter itself is actual as what has the readiness to receive a new form, but only potentially what it will become. In this sense it exists in itself, while also being absent in relation to what may come next.

A feature that depends on something else must come after the thing it belongs to, just as matter depends on form. Such a feature is even more dependent than matter, since matter at least has some priority in relation to form. So no dependent feature can be the first effect. God has no separate quality, whether eternal or newly added to Him. The Ashʿarites and Karrāmī theologians, for example, claimed that His will could be eternal or newly formed. The first thing after God must therefore be one being, independent in both what it is and what it does. It can only be a pure intellect, since matter has no actual existence, body has no unity, form and dependent features require something else in order to exist, and soul depends on something else in its action.

The second proof comes from the rule that many things cannot come directly from the One. The third proof uses the rule of the nobler possible being. Intellect is nobler than every other possible being. It is one level in the single reality of existence. The fourth proof is the natural fit between a cause and its effect. The fit between the first cause and its first effect must be the closest and most complete possible. The first effect must therefore be the noblest intellect and the simplest, brightest immaterial being after God.

The fifth proof concerns how a soul reaches the knowledge it has only in potential. When something has the ability to reach a perfection but has not yet reached it, something else must bring it from possibility to actuality. Otherwise, it would make itself complete, which is impossible: if it could do that, it would already be complete. It would also be both less complete and more complete than itself at once.

So the human soul cannot bring itself from basic, potential understanding to actual understanding, even when it has prepared itself through learning and practice. It needs an immaterial teacher and giver of forms between God and the souls that receive knowledge. This giver must be free of potential and change, or it too would need another being to complete it, leading to an endless chain. It cannot be God Himself without an intermediary, since there are many souls but God is absolutely one. So there must be an intellectual being between God and the souls that receive from Him.

The active intellect relates to the soul’s readiness for understanding as sunlight relates to the eye. Sunlight makes sight actual, and makes the things seen visible. The eye and what it sees both become actual through the light. In the same way, the soul and what it understands become actual through the intellect that gives knowledge.

The sixth proof comes from the relation between matter and form. For matter to exist, it needs a form in general, not any one fixed kind of form. It also needs an immaterial intellect. When one form passes away, this intellect supplies another in its place. Matter can therefore remain one and the same individual through a changing succession of forms. The forms provide one kind of continuity as they replace one another; the enduring intellect provides another, unchanging kind. We explained this earlier when discussing how matter and form depend on one another.

passage-en-00742

The seventh proof comes from changing nature. Nature changes in its individual existence, though its kind remains the same. The cause of this change cannot be God directly, for He is one in every respect. Nor can it be another changing nature: that would leave us asking the same question again and lead either to an endless chain of causes or to causes circling back on themselves. It cannot be a soul, because the soul, insofar as it is tied to the body and develops through it, also changes and passes from one state to another. Nor can the cause be matter, which receives rather than produces forms. It must be an immaterial intellect, a divine form and a noble angel.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00743

The eighth proof comes from desire and purpose. Every natural kind is drawn toward a final perfection that belongs to the world of intellect. Otherwise, the natural desire to reach completion would be pointless, and nature does nothing in vain. Some things may be prevented from reaching their goal, but such obstacles are not usual or lasting. The final perfections toward which things move cannot be souls, which still long for a more complete state, or God, who is one while these perfections are many. They must be intellects. Just as an intellectual being must stand between God and created things at the beginning of their descent, so intellectual beings must stand between created things and God at the end of their return.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00744

The ninth proof starts with beings whose nature is complete enough to receive existence without first becoming ready through matter. Their own possibility is enough for the Giver to bring them into being. They therefore come before time and before things that move, occupy places, or depend on bodily conditions. This is a priority in being, not an earlier date. Nothing in their nature prevents them from receiving existence, and nothing can prevent the Giver from giving it. They therefore receive existence without interruption.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00745

Other kinds of things need matter to be ready before any particular individual can exist. Their individuals depend on particular materials, places, and times. Yet their natures, considered as kinds rather than as individual members, also receive their existence continually from the Giver. The giving is constant even though its recipients, considered one by one, come into being and pass away. Thus the forms of different kinds flow from God continually, while the bodily world and the things within it arise in time after not existing.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00746

Since the First Reality is one, there must be immaterial intellects between Him and the different kinds of material things. These intellects have distinct ways of acting through which different kinds can receive existence. Matter can make many individuals of one kind, and different material conditions can distinguish those individuals. But matter and its readiness cannot, by themselves, account for the existence of different kinds with different natures.

passage-en-00747
This also proves that an intellectual world exists and contains many forms. These forms do not stand apart from God’s being; they are divine knowledge within the realm of His rule.

The tenth proof comes from the motion of the heavenly spheres. Anything that moves must be moved by something other than itself. Otherwise, the same thing would be both what is moved and what moves it, and what completes it would itself need completion. If the mover also moves, another mover is needed, and so on without end. We must reach a mover that does not move at all, an actual being that does not change by nature, force, divine direction, or choice. It moves the sphere either by giving it its first impulse or by serving as the beloved model that the moving sphere seeks to imitate.

passage-en-00749

Second, the circular motion of the heavenly spheres cannot be natural motion; it must come from a soul that knows and chooses. But the spheres do not have bodily appetites or anger. They need no food and have no enemy. Their movement must aim at an intellectual good. It cannot be a low or uncertain goal, and it cannot be a bodily benefit. It must be a high intellectual perfection. The spheres move not to become God, but to imitate many beloved intellects. All seek the First Beloved in their shared circular movement, but each also has its own beloved, which guides its particular movement and helps it draw nearer to God.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00750

Third, the heavenly motions never stop. Their source must have unlimited power. No bodily power, whether in a soul or in a form within matter, can produce endless motion. So their source must be an immaterial power. These three arguments show that there are intellects, not just one.

The eleventh proof comes from the agreement between true judgments in our minds and what is true in itself. We know that some judgments are true and match reality, while others held by ignorant people do not. This match can occur only between two different things that agree in the relevant respect. Both kinds of judgment exist in the mind, but only true judgments also match something outside our minds. That reality is what we call “what is true in itself.”

passage-en-00752

This reality outside us must either stand on its own or exist within something else. If it stands on its own, it is either physical or not physical. It cannot be physical. These judgments do not belong to any place or time, but everything physical has a place and time. We can also know that they match even when we know nothing about a physical thing. And we grasp these judgments through intellect; we grasp physical things through the senses. The reality cannot be a nonphysical being standing on its own either, since that would be Plato’s separate Forms.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00753

So the truth our judgments match must exist within something that does not divide. It cannot exist there only as a possibility, even if some judgments are only possible in our minds. A possible truth cannot match a truth that is already real. Nor can it change from possibility into actuality, because these truths must be true forever, without change or limits of time and place. Their source must also exist in an unchanging way. So there must be an independent, nonphysical being that contains all the truths our minds can reach—the truths that remain unchanged forever.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00754

That being cannot be God, who is absolutely one. It must contain many truths, and God cannot contain many things as parts or as separate objects of knowledge. So there must be another being, which we may call the Universal Intellect. The Qur'an calls it the Preserved Tablet, or the Clear Book that contains all things, fresh and dry. This is what I wanted to establish.

We accept Plato’s separate Forms, as we have already explained, but this proof does not depend on them. It establishes a world of intellect in which the enduring truths are present, whether they exist within an intellectual being or stand on their own.

passage-en-00756

The twelfth proof comes from the difference between complete and incomplete beings. In thought, things fall into four groups: complete or incomplete; the complete may be more than complete or simply complete; the incomplete may be able to reach completion by itself, with something that belongs to it, or only with something outside it. Material things are incomplete. The heavenly spheres can reach their own completion. God is beyond complete. There must therefore be a complete being between God and material things: the intellect. If God, who is beyond complete, directly created something incomplete, there would be no fit between the Giver and what receives existence. There would also be a gap in the order of existence. Our rule about the lower possible being has already shown that no level can be skipped.

As support, Aristotle’s school says in the tenth book of Theology of Aristotle:
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00758

The One, who has no parts, is the cause of all things. He is not any one of them, but their beginning. He is not the things, but all things are in Him. They all flow from Him, are held together by Him, and return to Him. If someone asks how all things can come from the simple One, who has no two-ness or multiplicity in any respect, we answer: because He is absolutely one and simple, with none of the things in Him. Precisely because He is absolutely one, all things flow from Him. Since He has no separate nature, all natures flow from Him.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00759

In short: because the One is not any one thing, all things are seen to come from Him. Yet the first nature to flow from Him without an intermediary is the nature of intellect. From it, all the natures of the higher and lower worlds flow. The pure One is beyond complete perfection; the world of sense is incomplete, made by the complete intellect. The intellect is complete because it comes from the One who is beyond complete. What is beyond complete cannot make something incomplete without an intermediary, and one complete being cannot make another equal to itself. The maker must be lower than what it makes.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00760

You are now prepared to understand this teacher’s words. When he says that “no separate nature” flows from the One, he likely means no separate existence, not no general nature. A general nature is not made. He means an individual existence that is distinct from other individual existences. Created beings each have existence limited by a degree of perfection, so each differs from the others. God’s existence is unlimited in power and intensity. It contains every level of existence and has nothing outside it to be set against it. Where God is, all things are in Him; where any created thing is, God is with it. The Qur'an says, “He is God in heaven and God on earth,” “He is with you wherever you are,” and “There is no private talk among three without Him being the fourth, or among five without Him being the sixth.” A saying reliably attributed to ʿAlī puts it this way: “He is with every thing, but not by being beside it; and He is other than every thing, but not by being apart from it.”
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00761

These are the proofs for the separate intellect and its world. I will later explain how many intellects there are, how well ordered their world is, and how it contains every kind found here, with many further perfections. I have already mentioned this in the discussion of nature.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00762

We have another way to show that intellectual forms are stored in the world of intellect. God says, “There is nothing whose storehouses are not with Us,” and, “To God belong the storehouses of the heavens and earth.” We may know something, forget it completely, and need to learn it again. Or we may lose sight of it for a time, then remember it without learning it again. In both cases, the image of the thing is no longer present in our active awareness. If it were there, we would know it, since knowing means that the image of a thing is present to the knowing power.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00763

But the two cases differ. When we lose sight of something but can remember it without new learning, its image has left our active awareness but remains in a power that keeps it. When we forget it completely, it has left both. In the second case, the mind has lost its readiness to connect with the power that gives knowledge. The senses can be divided, so one place in the brain may receive images while another keeps them. This is the common account. But our intellect cannot be divided into one place for receiving knowledge and another for keeping it.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00764

So a separate intellectual being must store the images our minds understand. When the soul turns toward it, it receives an image that fits its nature. When the soul turns toward the body or to another image, the earlier one disappears from awareness. It is like a mirror that has been cleaned and turned toward a picture: while it faces the picture, the image appears in it, or the light from the picture reaches it. This is how two philosophers explain the relation between the mind and the intellectual world: one says the image shines into us, the other that it flows into us. I have already said that neither account is the one I accept. I say that the soul joins with the intellectual being itself.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00765

If the mind has been cleared and the heart made pure, it keeps the ability to reconnect with the image it once understood. It can recall it without learning it again. The image was out of mind, but not forgotten. The mind has kept its connection and its readiness to receive it. If the mind becomes clouded again by the body and nature, it needs new effort to clear the barrier and reconnect. So there is an intellectual being that keeps all the forms our minds can understand. This is what I wanted to prove.

1. Closing clarification: Resolving a difficult objection
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter

This argument has an objection about lapses of attention and forgetting. Some thinkers found it so difficult that one of Tusi’s students could not answer it. Ḥillī recounts the exchange in his commentary on The Guide to Belief:
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00768

While I was studying with him, I once asked what people mean when they say that a judgment in the mind is true when it matches what is true in itself. What is true in itself is either something in the mind or something outside it, but he had rejected both. He replied that “what is true in itself” means the Active Intellect. Every image or judgment in the mind is true if it matches the images impressed in the Active Intellect; otherwise it is false. I objected that the philosophers themselves must then say false images are impressed in the Active Intellect. They argued that it exists by pointing to the difference between losing sight of an idea and forgetting it. Losing sight means an idea leaves the knowing intellect but remains in the power that keeps it; forgetting means it leaves both. This can happen with sensory images, they say, but in the case of ideas it happens when the mind loses its readiness to receive knowledge. Yet we can lose sight of and forget false ideas too.

passage-en-00769
He did not give a satisfactory answer.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00770
Dawānī answers that the Active Intellect stores both true and false ideas, but it agrees with and affirms only the true ones. It keeps false ideas only as pictures, without accepting them as true.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00771

I say that ideas in the Active Intellect are more settled and certain than those in our minds. When two things are linked in our minds, the link may be weak because its cause or proof is weak. We may not know whether they truly belong together, or the link may be false. But when they are linked in the Active Intellect, their connection is firm and necessary, like the connection between things in the world.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00772

Second, imagining and affirming are two kinds of knowledge that arise in our changing, bodily minds. The higher sources of knowledge, and God’s own knowledge, are neither pictures in a mind nor judgments. They are the presence of the knower and the known to each other. Their necessary qualities are present with them, without any further act of learning or creation, as our knowledge of ourselves and our own qualities is present with us.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00773

To settle this objection, I must first explain that every lasting ability in the human soul—whether it is a way of knowing or a practical skill such as writing, trading, or farming—comes from a special link between the soul and the Active Intellect. It comes from the Active Intellect through one of its active features. Different kinds of things cannot arise only because their receivers differ or can receive different things. They must have either many separate intellectual causes, as Plato’s followers say, or many active features in the last intellect, as Aristotle’s followers say.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00774

The Active Intellect contains all these different abilities in a higher and simpler way. This is true even of things called bad, since their badness lies in the loss or absence of something else. Acts such as adultery and theft are real actions, even though they harm what ought to be protected. A lie and a firmly held false belief are also real states in the soul; in themselves, they are among the things a living creature can do. They become harmful when compared with a higher soul that needs steady knowledge and truth. In themselves, they are positive states, but in relation to that higher soul they are faults.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00775

Once this is clear, not every ability or quality in the human soul must exist in exactly the same form in the Active Intellect. It is enough that something there fits each one. Repeated attention to true knowledge connects the soul to one side of the Active Intellect. In the same way, a false belief or a strong focus on it can connect the soul to another side. The side it reaches does not need to be the very same false statement. There only needs to be a feature that fits it. This is what it means to say that the intellectual world stores the forms of things and that the soul can recover them.
Station Nine: God’s creative act and the existence of beings whose existence does not depend on physical matter
passage-en-00776

We have explained more than once that images in the simple intellect are not stored as many separate images, as they are in physical matter or in the detailed imagination. The world of intellect is too full and complete for that kind of separation, absence, and division.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00777
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00778

Nothing outside Him ever keeps God from acting, even though the world is always changing, coming into being, and passing away. The only things that never perish, diminish, or run out are God’s complete words and lasting knowledge. As we have often said, these do not belong to the world or to anything apart from the Real.

passage-en-00779
I. Why this question matters, and why God’s unceasing giving is compatible with a world that comes into being and changes
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00780

This is one of the most important questions in both philosophy and religion. We cannot know God, affirm His oneness, or understand Him as free from multiplicity and defect unless we grasp it clearly, in a way that fits sound reasoning and the teachings of the prophets. Many people with little understanding imagine that philosophy and rational inquiry conflict with divine law and the prophets’ teachings. They also assume that the great philosophers of old taught that the whole world is eternal: that the heavens, stars, their forms and matter, and even the matter and kinds of earthly elements have always existed as the same individual things, without ever passing away or coming into being. As we explained when discussing substance and its kinds, this is a false charge against those early philosophers. Their view was not the crude one attributed to them, which conflicts with the prophets and their followers.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00781

They did hold that God’s generosity is eternal and His outpouring never stops. But the world itself is renewed with every breath. This is one meaning of the verse, “Every day He is at work”: His acts and the appearances of His names are always new, as we have already explained. A changing effect can depend on an eternal, unchanging cause only if it is continually renewed: things come to be and endure gradually, while change and loss continue without a break. People commonly say the same about motion: it is a gradual process that exists bit by bit and passes away bit by bit.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00782

In our view, however, motion is not itself an independently existing thing. It is an idea we use for the gradual passage from possibility to actuality. Like other ideas we form by considering real things, it describes an actual thing whose existence unfolds step by step. That thing’s existence is therefore gradual; as it comes to be, it also passes away. Each moment ends as the next begins, and that unbroken succession is what we call continuity. Motion itself does not move. It means that something else is coming into actuality little by little. Otherwise, motion would need another motion to move it, and another after that, without end.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00783

What changes gradually, in itself, are certain kinds of things. The usual account lists four: quantity, quality, place, and position. A closer account adds substance as a fifth, because material natures and souls joined to natural bodies change in their very being, as we have proved. Every bodily thing in this world—simple or composite, form or matter, heavenly or earthly, soul or nature—has a time before which it did not exist. Each particular existence is preceded by a past without that thing. At the beginning of time there were no bodily individuals or natural beings. Taken one by one, together, or as a complete collection, every one of them was preceded by absence. Each is therefore something that came to be. None is one individual that has existed continuously with an unchanging identity.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00784

The so-called “universal nature”—what a kind of thing is, considered without choosing any one example—does not have its own existence, unity, plurality, continuity, or beginning apart from its individual examples. It follows those examples in every respect: it exists through their existence, is one through their unity, many through their plurality, old through their age, and new through their coming to be.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00785

Once reason shows that every individual example came to be, the universal nature must also be new in reality. It may not be new when we consider only what it means in itself, but for the same reason it is not eternal in itself either. This reveals that a common claim among philosophers—that kinds are eternal because their individual examples succeed one another—is mistaken. It confuses the idea of a thing with the thing itself. It also confuses being one in number with being one in meaning.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00786

Many people think this means that one and the same thing remains in existence while different features come and go. When one feature disappears, the underlying thing remains and receives another feature. They imagine it as one body that is white at one time and black at another, hot at one time and cold at another. The body, they say, is the same throughout all these changes.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00787

But this is a serious mistake. Avicenna criticized those who claimed that a universal nature exists outside the mind as one thing, multiplied by its attachments, appearing in many places and at many times. He said that a universal meaning does not relate to its individual examples as one father relates to many sons, but as different fathers relate to different sons. A person does not merely share one separate “humanity” with everyone else. Each person’s humanity is a distinct individual, different in number from everyone else’s. What people share exists only as a meaning in the mind. We discussed this earlier when examining what things are.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00788

A further point follows. Theologians tried to prove that motion, time, and the chain of events have a beginning and an end by comparing their parts and relations. Some followers of the philosophers objected that these successive events never exist together, either in the world or in the imagination, so they cannot be compared all at once or judged to have an endpoint. But they missed a key point: if the whole chain of events does not exist as one thing, we cannot call that whole eternal or without limit either. How, then, can they say that motion and time are eternal, or that events have no beginning?
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00789

The right answer is that “eternal” and “without limit” do not apply to the chain as one existing thing. Nor do “begun” and “finite” apply to that nonexistent whole as though it were a single object. We can, however, say positively of each particular motion, moment of time, and event that it began and has an end. This does not prove that the collection as a whole began. What is true of every member does not always transfer to a collection as one thing. Nor does it prove that the whole collection is eternal, as some claim, or that the universal nature is eternal.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00790

Someone might object: if the whole has no end, then it must be infinite; and if a universal nature is not new in itself, then it must be eternal in itself. In answer to the first claim, something that does not exist cannot have any property. A positive claim needs an existing subject. So how could we say of a nonexistent whole that it has some feature, whether that feature is something real or the absence of something—such as blindness, lack of sight, or lack of writing?
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00791

A nonexistent thing lacks sight, but it also lacks the condition “not seeing.” The opposite of saying that a thing sees is not to say that it positively has “not-seeing”; it is to deny that seeing belongs to it at all. In the same way, both writing and not-writing are denied of what does not exist. Neither is a property it possesses.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00792

As for the second claim, when we say that a universal nature is not new in itself, we mean that the idea of what a thing is does not include its having come to be. We do not mean that it never comes to be in reality. In fact, it does come to be, because each individual example of it does. Whatever is true of each example is true of that nature as it exists through those examples.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00793

Even if we grant that a nature, considered in itself, is neither new nor old, it does not follow that it must be old or eternal. As we explained earlier, when we consider what a thing is by itself, we deny both sides of a pair of opposites. The kinds whose individual examples come and go are, in reality, new; they are not eternal or everlasting. If a kind were eternal in reality, at least one of its individual examples would have to be eternal, since the kind exists only through its examples. A kind has no feature apart from the features of its examples. Since none of them is eternal or everlasting, neither is the kind.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00794

If we ask whether the kind is eternal or new in itself, we must deny both: in itself it is neither eternal nor new, neither without a beginning nor beginning, neither endless nor finite. It has these features in reality only through its existence in individual examples.

passage-en-00795
II. Another proof that bodies come into being
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00796

Here is another way to prove that bodies came into being, different from the argument we gave earlier when discussing substance. Anything described by a quality must not, in its own existence and in the state in which it can receive that quality, already have the opposite quality. Otherwise one thing would have two conflicting qualities at once, either in thought or in reality.
Station Ten: God’s unceasing generosity and eternal power
passage-en-00797

The first kind of example is what a thing is, considered in itself, and its relation to existence. If a thing’s nature were already nonexistent in itself, existence could not come to belong to it. To receive either existence or nonexistence, its nature must first be undecided between the two. The second kind is a bodily size or extension received by basic matter. Matter cannot already be fixed as having no size or extension; otherwise it could not receive extension and become measurable. The same goes for position and place. If a thing gains a position or place, it cannot already exist in a way that rules both out. Something that exists without size, position, or place is an intelligible, nonbodily thing. How, then, could it become a body and take on these features?
